verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Censure of Craving': the poet to his own hope.
verse_text.line: I swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart. Hope, how much longer will you make me dance?
verse_text.translation: I somehow put up with the taunts of the wicked while trying to please them; I held back my tears and laughed with an empty heart; I folded my hands even before people whose minds were numbed by money. Hope, futile hope, how much more will you make me dance?

reading: You skipped for the promotion again and find yourself wondering if they are right about you. Bhartrihari speaks to hope itself, asking how much longer it will make him dance after swallowing insults and forcing laughter with an empty heart. Today, that empty laughter might sit in the room where the decision was made, reminding you that the cost of waiting for their approval is real.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to his own hope in the Censure of Craving. He has spent his life digging for treasure and humbling himself before kings. Now he lists the taunts he swallowed and the tears he held back. He forced laughter with an empty heart and folded his hands before men numbed by money. He asks hope how much longer it will make him dance in this way. The verse proposes that we often think we are chasing goals, but really the chase is using up our lives. You are wondering if they are right about you after being passed over again. The verse names the cost of waiting for approval you do not yet have.

verse_text.speaker: Manu
verse_text.setting: Manu, offered any boon after years of austerity, hesitates to ask for what he truly wants.
verse_text.line: Like a poor man before the wishing tree, we hesitate to ask for what we really want.
verse_text.translation: Like a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power, so doubt rises in my heart.

reading: You feel uneasy because your manager keeps handing visible projects to others, and you wonder if you are simply not leadership material. The verse says that like a poor man before the wishing tree, we hesitate to ask for what we really want, not knowing its power, so doubt rises in the heart. Today, that doubt may be hiding the very projects you want, not because you lack worth, but because you hesitate to name the wish. You can still tell your manager plainly which work you want to lead.
meaning: King Manu speaks to Lord Vishnu after years of austerity in the forest. Vishnu has appeared and told him to ask for any boon. Manu feels that seeing the Lord's feet already fulfils every wish, yet one great longing remains. He compares himself to a poor man who finds a wishing tree but hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power. He admits that doubt rises in his heart because he feels too small to make the request. You carry the sense that you are not leadership material because your manager keeps giving visible projects to others. The verse shows that hesitation can hide what you want, not a lack of worth inside you.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna, seeing his own family in the enemy ranks, collapses in grief before the battle.
verse_text.line: Shaking limbs, a dry mouth, a racing body: the Gita opens with a panic attack, not a hero.
verse_text.translation: My limbs give way, my mouth is parched, my body trembles and my hair stands on end.

reading: Your boss pulls out your mistake in front of everyone, and now you feel useless. In the Gita, Arjuna tells Krishna that his limbs give way, his mouth is dry, his body trembles and his hair stands on end. That same panic can live in your body today when work feels unsafe, and naming it is a honest witness to what is happening right now.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the battlefield. He has just seen his own family standing in the enemy ranks. He collapses in grief and fear. His limbs shake, his mouth goes dry, his body trembles and his hair stands on end. The verse is his honest report of his body breaking down under the weight of what he sees. It proposes that even the strongest people can freeze. The teaching begins with that breakdown, not with a hero. That same panic lives in your body when your boss calls out your mistake in front of everyone. Naming it is an honest witness to what is happening right now.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: Since the breakup you have realised your friends were really his friends, and weekends are just you now. Krishna tells Arjuna, See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me. In a season when connection feels narrowed to one, this verse names a bond that distance cannot break, pointing to a presence that remains even when human closeness shifts.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just described the yogi who sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self. Now he restates this in his own voice. He says that whoever sees him everywhere and sees everything within him will never be lost to him, and he will never be lost to that person. The verse proposes that a steady gaze which finds the one presence in all things, and all things within that presence, settles the mind through moderation and gentle return. Since your friends were really his friends, your circle has narrowed sharply. This verse speaks of a bond that distance cannot break, even when human closeness shifts.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: Starting fresh in a new city after your divorce, you do not know a single person around you. Krishna tells Arjuna that whoever sees him everywhere and sees everything in him is never lost to him, and he is never lost to them. In this unfamiliar place, that bond can be a quiet anchor: the divine never loses sight of you here, just as you carry the familiar within you.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the field of instruction. He has just described the one who sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self. Now he restates this in his own voice. He says that whoever sees him everywhere and sees everything resting in him will never be lost to him, and he will never be lost to that person. The idea is that a steady, wide attention keeps the bond unbroken. After your divorce and your move, you are in a place where no one knows your name. That wide attention can be a quiet way to feel held even when the streets around you are empty.

verse_text.speaker: the gopis
verse_text.setting: The women of Braj, after Krishna has left, on missing him.
verse_text.line: "Since he left, it has been monsoon in our eyes."
verse_text.translation: Night and day our eyes keep raining. Ever since Shyam went away, it is always the rainy season for us.

reading: You feel empty because your closest friend moved abroad and you barely talk now, and you did not realise how much of your life was him. The gopis say that since he left, it has been monsoon in their eyes, night and day their eyes keep raining. This speaks to you today because your missing him can feel like weather that does not lift, and saying that plainly is part of still loving him.
meaning: The women of Braj speak these lines after Krishna leaves. They tell a friend that night and day their eyes keep raining. Ever since Shyam went away, it is always the rainy season for them. The verse says that weeping for someone you miss is allowed. The loss is so total that tears become a season rather than a single event. Your missing him can feel like weather that does not lift, and saying that plainly is part of still loving him.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: You describe every day as firefighting with nothing left in the tank. Bali, sitting by his window, says again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks, and to a thinking person this feels like a mockery. Today, that same loop may sit heavily with you, not because the work itself is empty, but because the repetition has outlasted its sense. When the next alarm sounds, notice the tasks themselves as they are, without asking them to mean more than they do.
meaning: The demon king Bali has ruled the three worlds for ages. One day he sits by his window and notices he is doing the same things again and again, day after day and night after night. He tells himself that to a thinking person this endless repetition feels like a mockery. The verse proposes that when life becomes a loop, the work is not to do more of it but to master the mind that runs it. You have been firefighting for so long that the repetition has drained your sense of purpose. Bali names the same weariness, and the verse points toward the mind behind the tasks rather than the tasks themselves.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You feel the weight of work pressure that never eases, and now the fatigue keeps you pinned to the bed even on weekends. Krishna tells Arjuna that contact with the world brings heat and cold, pleasure and pain, and these come and go without lasting. Today, this can meet the exhaustion in your body by naming it as something that touches and moves on, leaving room for the stillness of the bed to hold you until it passes.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after Arjuna has grieved the coming battle. Arjuna stands on the field fearing he will kill his own kin. Krishna has just told him that the self inside never dies and simply changes bodies like clothes. Now Arjuna still feels the coming heat and cold of war. Krishna tells him that sense contact brings pleasure and pain, and these arrive and depart like weather. They do not last. Arjuna must bear them without letting either joy or grief carry him away. Your work pressure and the fatigue that pins you down are real. They touch you through your senses and your body, and they too arrive and depart without lasting forever.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You cannot sleep while your mind spins on whether the launch will work. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, as hard to hold as the wind. This restlessness does not mean the launch is doomed; it simply names the force you are facing while you wait for morning.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna describes the highest yogi as one who feels the joy and pain of all beings as his own. Arjuna objects that such steady evenness cannot last. He says the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, and as hard to hold as the wind. The Gita takes this complaint seriously. It proposes that practice and letting go can train the mind. Your mind is spinning on the launch because it is doing exactly what Arjuna named. The restlessness is real, but it is not proof that the launch will fail.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse_text.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
verse_text.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.

reading: You feel smaller beside colleagues who hold MBAs while you carry only experience, and each time it seems you fall short. Krishna tells Arjuna to raise himself by his own self and not let himself sink, for the self alone is the friend of the self. Today, your own steady regard can be the ground that holds you, lifting you up instead of letting those comparisons drag you down.

verse_text.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 7, Epistles – Third Series, LII, p. 525
verse_text.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse_text.listener: Mrs. Blodgett ('Aunt Roxy'), his hostess in Los Angeles
verse_text.setting: Letter of 2 May 1900, in failing health, near the end of his second American tour.
verse_text.line: I just want a bit of peace badly — pray for me.
verse_text.translation: Well, dear good mother, may all blessings attend you and peace. I just want a bit of peace badly — pray for me. With love to Kate,

reading: You wake every evening to homework battles with your 6-year-old and then hate yourself after losing your temper. Swami Vivekananda wrote plainly, 'I just want a bit of peace badly — pray for me.' That same honest weariness can surface for you today, asking to be named without shame.
meaning: Swami Vivekananda wrote this to Mrs Blodgett, his hostess in Los Angeles, on the second of May nineteen hundred. He was in failing health after six months of intense lecturing across America. His heart and kidneys were sound, yet he had relapsed into nervous exhaustion and fever. He told her he would rest a few days in the country before going to Chicago. He closed by asking her for a bit of peace and for her prayers. Your anger at the homework table is not a moral flaw. It is the plain signal of a body running on empty after a long day of work and care.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: Every week the slamming doors and yelling leave you both feeling awful. The Yoga Vasishtha describes a mind caught on endless waves of tasks, repeating 'done this, doing this, must do that,' until the bird of the mind faints in its own net of reckonings. Today, the noise of those weekly clashes can remind you that the loop itself is exhausting the mind, not only the moment in the hallway.
meaning: In the Yoga Vasishtha, two old friends meet again after years apart. Bhasa admits to Vilasa that he never found peace. He says the mind is carried along on endless waves of tasks. It never rests because it keeps counting what is done, what is being done, and what must still be done. The depths of the mind dance with worry. The bird of the mind gets tangled in a net of reckonings and faints. Your weeks of slamming doors and yelling are part of that same endless list. The verse points to the loop itself, not only the hallway moment.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From the section on the wicked: the impossible position of anyone who serves a master.
verse_text.line: Quiet, you're dull; talkative, a show-off; patient, weak. Serving a boss is harder than yoga.
verse_text.translation: Keep quiet and you are dumb; speak well and you are a babbler or a windbag; stay close and you are pushy; keep away and you lack confidence; be patient and you are a coward; refuse to put up with things and you are ill-bred. The duty of serving another is deep indeed, beyond the reach even of yogis.

reading: You are furious because your lead dumped his work on you and you snapped in standup, and now you feel like the problem. Bhartrihari writes that serving a boss means any behaviour can be read as a fault: keep quiet and you are dull, speak and you are a show-off. This double bind speaks to you today, because the trap lies in the position itself, not in you. In your standup, the fault was the unfair load, not your snap.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to the reader from his section on wicked people. He describes the courtier who serves a cruel master. The master twists every action into a fault. Stay silent and you are dull. Speak and you are a windbag. Stay close and you are pushy. Keep away and you lack confidence. Be patient and you are weak. Refuse the abuse and you are ill bred. Serving another in such a place is harder than yoga. Even sages cannot master it. Your lead dumped his work on you and you snapped in standup. Now you carry the blame. The verse says the trap is the position, not your reaction.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
verse_text.line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verse_text.translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.

reading: You are waiting on emergency leave while your dad is in hospice in Delhi. Krishna, far from home, tells his mother Yashoda that since he left, no one has called him by his pet name, and he has not had breakfast or warm milk. In your waiting, the absence of ordinary tenderness—being known simply by your home name, being fed—may ache more than the distance itself.
meaning: Krishna sends a message through to his foster mother Yashoda. He is far from home in Mathura after killing. He tells her to stay well and that the two brothers will come in four or five days. He adds that since the day he left, no one has called him Kanhaiya. He has not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk in the evening. The verse shows that missing home is love. It carries the simple truth that a pet name and a mother's food mark a belonging that a palace cannot replace. Your waiting for leave holds the same ache. The ordinary tenderness of being called by your home name and being fed is what you miss while you wait in Delhi.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: The self was never born and never dies. It is not killed when the body is.
verse_text.translation: It is never born and never dies; having been, it will not cease to be. Unborn, eternal, constant and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.

reading: You are watching your mother slowly leave as her cancer reaches the final stage. Krishna tells Arjuna that the self was never born and never dies; it is not slain when the body is slain. Today, as you stand beside her fading form, this speaks to the reality that what made her who she was was never born and does not end with her body. Let this truth sit quietly beside the grief you carry as you care for her.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is shaken by the thought of fighting his own kin. Krishna tells him that the core of a person, the self, has no birth and no death. It existed before and will exist after. The body changes and perishes, but the self is untouched by that ending. The verse proposes that what a person truly is outlasts every change a body goes through. Your mother is fading, and you feel lost in the watching. This verse points to the part of her that was never born and will not end with her body.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
verse_text.line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verse_text.translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.

reading: You missed your mom's surgery because leave was denied, and she says it is fine, yet the thought will not leave you. Krishna, far from home, tells Yashoda that since he left, no one has called him by his pet name, and he has gone without his morning breakfast or evening warm milk. In your distance from her now, this speaks of the small tendernesses you both miss, not of any fault on your side.
meaning: Krishna sends a message through to his foster mother Yashoda. He is far away in Mathura after killing. He tells her to stay well and that he and his brother will visit in four or five days. He adds that since the day he left home, no one has called him by his pet name Kanhaiya. He also says he has not eaten morning breakfast or evening warm milk. The verse shows that missing home is love. It means that love in separation runs both ways. The prince misses the ordinary tenderness of home. Your mother says she is fine, but you carry the weight of missing her surgery. This verse names the small tendernesses that vanish in distance. It shows that your absence hurts her too, not as blame but as shared loss.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: Arjuna asks this, and many of us ask it too: what pushes a person to do wrong, even unwillingly, as if forced? If you're carrying something you did, you've probably asked it at night. The Gita treats the question as worth a full answer.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong against their own will, as if pushed by some outside force. Krishna answers that it is desire. When desire is blocked, it turns into anger. That anger clouds a person's wisdom. The verse proposes that a person can see this pattern clearly and then master it. You spoke in anger and now you cannot meet your father's eyes. The verse names the push behind that moment, not to condemn you, but to show where it came from.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: You yelled at your grandmother when she asked the same question for the fifth time, and she went quiet. Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against his will, as if pushed by force. The verse speaks to your fear of your own temper by naming that inner pull without calling you wicked for it. You can sit with the fact that she went quiet, and with Arjuna’s honest question, as your starting point today.
meaning: Arjuna, the warrior, asks Krishna, his guide, why a person does wrong even when he does not want to, as if pushed by some outside force. Krishna answers that it is desire left unmet. That desire turns into anger. Anger clouds a person's judgment like smoke over a flame. The verse proposes that you see this pull clearly. Once you see it, you can master it. Your fear of your own temper comes from a real inner pull, not from a wicked core. You can start here without calling yourself bad.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: You lost the partnership after saying unforgivable things in a rage, and now the guilt stays. Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born, and from attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger. The anger that flared and cost you the partnership grew from something you kept dwelling on before the snap. That guilt staying with you points to the dwelling that fed the fire, long before the words were spoken.
meaning: Krishna is answering Arjuna, who has just asked what a person of steady mind looks like in speech, posture and walk. Krishna traces how a person loses that steadiness. When someone dwells on an object, attachment to it is born. That attachment hardens into wanting. When that wanting is blocked, it turns into anger. This is the chain that ruins a composed life.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You dropped out and now nothing seems worth the effort. Young Rama asks, What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for? This verse meets your emptiness as a real, open question rather than a dead end, inviting you to sit with who you are beneath the lack of direction.
meaning: Young Rama stands in his father's court after returning from his travels. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha are there, and Rama has just been asked why he seems so low. He speaks his honest lament. He asks what kingship and pleasure mean to him, who he really is, and what all this is for. He says if everything is unreal, let it be unreal, and asks whose it is and what anyone has truly gained. The text treats this questioning as the healthy beginning of inquiry, not as a final answer. Your emptiness after dropping out is not a failure to be fixed. It is the same honest opening Rama named, asking what matters when the old path is gone.

verse_text.speaker: Rama's attendant
verse_text.setting: Rama's attendants describe the prince's withdrawal to his worried father.
verse_text.line: He no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just goes quiet.
verse_text.translation: He doesn't light up at jokes, doesn't lose himself in pleasures, doesn't stay with his work; he just keeps silent.

reading: You put in so much effort and still nothing came of it, and now nothing feels like it matters. In the Yoga Vasishtha, Rama's attendants tell King Dasharatha that the prince no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work; he simply keeps silent. That quiet withdrawal speaks to the emptiness you carry today. It is okay that work no longer holds your spark, and you do not have to force the old interest back.
meaning: Dasharatha asks his servants for news of Rama after the prince returns from a long pilgrimage. They report that the sixteen year old heir no longer laughs at jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his duties. He simply keeps silent. The text treats this quiet withdrawal as a serious sign that something inside him has shifted, opening the way for deeper questions if others help him through it. Your own long effort brought no reward, so the work that once mattered now feels hollow. That silence is a real response, not a failure on your part.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: After 15 years of 12-hour days, the business stands but the feeling of nothing remains. Bali, sitting by his window, says again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks, and to a thinking person this feels like a mockery. That weariness you carry today is the verse's own witness: the loop has become visible, and in that visibility there is a quiet, real opening.
meaning: The demon king Bali has ruled the three worlds for ages. One day he sits by his window and notices he is doing the same things day after day, night after night. He speaks to himself and says the daily round is a chain of tasks that repeats without end. To a thinking person this repetition feels like a mockery. The verse proposes that when life feels like a loop, the work is not more of it but mastering the mind that runs it. You built this business through fifteen years of long days, and now the structure stands while the feeling inside it has gone flat. The verse names that exact weariness without asking you to fix it today.

verse_text.speaker: Nidagha
verse_text.setting: Nidagha on craving.
verse_text.line: Every good quality I take up, craving gnaws through, like a mouse chewing a string.
verse_text.translation: Whatever good quality I take refuge in, great sage, craving cuts it away, as a mouse gnaws through a string.

reading: You plan to study after work but end up scrolling till 1am. The Maha Upanishad speaks of craving gnawing through every good quality like a mouse chewing a string. Even the resolve to study gets quietly frayed by that background wanting. Tonight, when the phone is in your hand, you might simply notice the nibbling instead of fighting it.
meaning: Nidagha speaks to Ribhu, his teacher, after returning from a pilgrimage feeling empty. He tells Ribhu that no matter what good quality he tries to hold onto, craving cuts it away. It works like a mouse gnawing through a string. The verse names a restless mind that quietly undoes every resolve we try to build. Your plan to study after work keeps fraying because a background wanting nibbles at it. The text does not call you weak. It points to the craving itself.

verse_text.speaker: Savitri
verse_text.setting: Knowing her husband will die in three days, Savitri takes a hard three-night vow; her father-in-law worries.
verse_text.line: I started this with determination, and determination will carry me to the end.
verse_text.translation: Don't be distressed, father. I will see this vow through. It was begun with determination, and determination is what carries it to the end.

reading: You have a firm resolve to prepare for GATE, yet starting each day consumes half your time. Savitri tells her father-in-law that she began this vow with determination, and that same determination will carry her to the end. Let that steady resolve be the force that carries your study sessions to completion today.
meaning: Savitri speaks to her blind father-in-law Dyumatsena. She knows her husband Satyavan will die in three days. She has begun a harsh three-night vow without food. Dyumatsena worries at its severity. Savitri tells him not to grieve. She says she started this vow with determination, and that same determination will carry it to the end. Your resolve for GATE is real. The same force that set you on this path can see your daily sessions through to completion.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Whatever a respected person does, others copy. The standard you set is the one people follow.
verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

reading: With your business at its best year ever, you want to keep your feet on the ground. Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a respected person does, others copy, and the standard you set is the one people follow. Your conduct now quietly shapes how those around you handle their own work, so your groundedness becomes a living example for them.
meaning: Krishna speaks this to Arjuna while they are together on the field. Arjuna has been wondering why anyone should act when they already have enough. Krishna answers that people look to those they respect and copy what those people do. He means that a leader does not need to preach. Their everyday conduct becomes the rule that everyone else follows.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You feel peaceful and thankful that everything is good. Bhartrihari wonders at his freedom to wander, food eaten without humiliation, good company, and learning that brings only calm, asking what generous austerity ripened into this. Today, your quiet morning and self-respecting ease can meet that same wonder, not as a reward earned, but as a gentle mystery you already hold.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines from his Worship of Shiva to the reader. He has just noted that moonlight, poetry and good company lose their charm once the mind sees how fleeting they are, and that the wise leave palaces for the forest. He then lists the goods of a simple renunciant life: freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, and a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long. Your peaceful gratitude already holds the same goods Bhartrihari names, and you can meet them with the same quiet wonder.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: You feel drawn to Krishna in a way you didn't expect. Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people worship him: those in distress, those curious, those in need, and the wise. Your unexpected pull toward the divine fits among these welcomed doors, and it can rest with you today as a quiet sign of belonging.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that deluded people do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. These are the distressed, the curious, those in need, and the wise. He says all four worship him. The verse proposes that whatever brings a person to the search is welcome. It does not demand a pure motive or a settled mind. Your unexpected pull toward Krishna is one of these welcomed doors. It does not need a reason or a label to count as real devotion.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: You have found calm through meditation and chanting, and now you wish to go deeper toward God. Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people turn to the divine: those in distress, those curious, those in need, and those wise. Your longing to go deeper is one of those welcome paths, and it can simply meet you at the next step of your practice.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after noting that wrongdoers and the deluded do not seek him. He explains that four kinds of good people do turn to the divine. These are the distressed, the curious, those in need, and the wise. The verse proposes that whatever brings a person to this search is welcome. It does not demand a single motive or a pure heart from the start. Your calm from meditation and chanting is already a real step. The longing to go deeper toward God fits naturally among the four welcome paths Krishna names.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: You long for the same joy in every moment that you feel while singing bhajans. Krishna tells Arjuna that people turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom, and calls all four kinds of seekers good. Whatever door brings you to that song today, it is already a worthy place to stand.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that the deluded do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. They are the distressed, the curious, those in need, and the wise. He says all four worship him. The verse proposes that whatever brings a person to the search is welcome. It does not demand a pure motive first. The same longing that rises while you sing now is already a worthy place to stand. It does not need to be bigger or purer to count.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse_text.line: Your work is yours to do; the results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop.
verse_text.translation: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to doing nothing.

reading: Karmaṇy evādhikāras te: your right is to the action. Fear of failure is a fear about the fruit, which was never given to you to control. Krishna also closes the escape route: don't let this make you stop acting. Care, prepare and aim well, then put the outcome down.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna stands between two armies, unsure whether to fight. Krishna tells him that his right extends only to the action itself. The outcome belongs to a larger order. One should do the work fully and then release ownership of what comes after. Inaction is not the answer. The teaching is about doing without clinging. Your launch is your action. The money that follows is not something you can hold in your hands. That gap between effort and outcome is where the anxiety lives.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You are carrying the work of half the team after cuts, waiting to see if you are next. Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go, and do not last; bear them patiently. Today, the weight on your shoulders is real, yet it is a contact that touches and moves on, not a permanent state. Rest in the fact that this waiting, like the work itself, has a beginning and an end.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These experiences arrive and depart on their own. They do not remain. Arjuna must bear them with patience and not let himself be swept away by either joy or sorrow. What is truly within you outlasts every loss and every passing pain. Your waiting has a shape and a limit. The weight you carry right now is real, but it is still a contact that touches and moves on, not a permanent state of who you are.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse_text.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.
verse_text.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.

reading: You carry the hurt of not being chosen, pushed out because you could not give a son. Krishna says his own relatives' harsh words churn his heart like fire-sticks, burning day after day. Your family's demand still burns, and the verse names that exact sting without asking you to carry it forever.
meaning: Krishna speaks to the sage Narada after growing weary of feuds inside his own clan. He tells Narada that he gives his kin half of what he owns and bears their harsh words, yet those words churn his heart like someone rubbing a fire-stick. The words keep burning him, day after day. The verse proposes that in family conflict, the only effective weapon is not force but gentleness, patience and respect. Your husband's family pushed him to leave you because you could not give them a son. The verse names that exact sting of being rejected by kin for not meeting their demand.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: The self was never born and never dies. It is not killed when the body is.
verse_text.translation: It is never born and never dies; having been, it will not cease to be. Unborn, eternal, constant and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.

reading: You carry the hurt of not being there for your father’s cremation. Krishna tells Arjuna that the self was never born and never dies; it is not slain when the body is slain. Let that truth sit beside your grief today, a steady presence next to the pain of your absence.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is shaken by the thought of fighting his own kin. Krishna tells him that the true self inside every person was never born and will never die. It does not perish when the body perishes. The self simply outlasts the body, like a person outlasting worn clothes. Your father's body reached its end while you were far away. The teaching points to what outlasts that ending, without asking you to set aside your sorrow.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: You are stretched across office deadlines, your son's exam prep, and a toddler. The Yoga Vasishtha speaks of a mind caught in 'done this, doing this, must do that,' carried along on endless waves so its depths dance with worry. Today, that reckoning may be exactly what you feel between tasks. A single breath, however brief, is the mind's own rest, not another item crossed off.
meaning: Bhasa speaks to his old friend Vilasa after they meet again as old men. Vilasa asks if Bhasa has found peace after years of hard austerity. Bhasa answers that there is no peace while the mind is swept along by endless tasks. He describes a mind caught in a loop of what is done, what is doing, and what must still be done. The mind becomes a bird tangled in a net of reckonings, fainting from the strain. The verse proposes that years of effort without inner understanding leave a person exactly where they started. Your stretch between work, your son, and the toddler mirrors that endless reckoning. The verse names the loop you are already inside.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: With work ramping up, daycare calling every other day about a fever, and your partner travelling, you are under constant pressure from all sides. Krishna tells Arjuna that contact of the senses with their objects brings heat and cold, pleasure and pain, and that they come and go and do not last. Today, this means the fever calls and the deadlines arrive as contacts that move on, and you can bear them patiently until they pass.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that the true self is never born and never dies. Yet the body meets cold and heat, pleasure and pain through the senses. These feelings come and go. They do not last. So Arjuna must bear them without being swept away. The pressure you feel is real, but it moves like weather. It is not the whole of who you are. You can carry it without letting it decide your next hour.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: You are starting your dream job on Monday, feeling excited yet terrified you will mess it up. Lakshmana tells Ram that there is no strength greater than enthusiasm, and for the one who has it, nothing is out of reach. That same energy can sit with your fear on Day One, turning the terror of messing up into the very force that carries you through your first tasks.
meaning: At Lake Pampa in spring, Ram is overcome by grief for Sita. Every bird and deer reminds him of her absence. Lakshman sees his brother sinking and tells him that enthusiasm is powerful. There is no strength greater than it. For the person who holds it, nothing in the world is out of reach. The verse proposes that resolute energy is the root of all effort, and by it alone the brothers will recover Sita. Your excitement for Monday carries the same fuel Lakshman names. It can sit right beside your fear without canceling it.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse_text.line: I'm confused about what's right. Tell me plainly what's best; I'm ready to learn.
verse_text.translation: My nature is stricken by weakness and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me for certain what is best for me. I am your student; I have come to you, teach me.

reading: You have been going back and forth on leaving your job for months, and it is all you think about, day and night. Arjuna tells Krishna that his mind is confused about what is right, and he asks plainly to be taught what is best. Today, your own uncertainty about what to do can be the place where you stop arguing with yourself and simply ask for clarity.
meaning: Arjuna stands on the battlefield and tells Krishna that his courage has failed him. He cannot tell which choice is better. He admits that his own mind is confused about what is right. He asks Krishna to teach him plainly what is best. He offers himself as a student ready to learn. Your own mind has been going in circles about this job, and that confusion is not a failure. It is the honest ground from which a clearer step can grow.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: You are carrying a full-time job, two young children, and nights when your husband is away, and the tiredness no longer leaves you even on holiday. Bhasa speaks of a mind caught on endless waves of tasks, fainting in a net of reckonings: 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do.' That same loop of running may be what you feel fraying inside you today, right in the middle of the next thing on your list.
meaning: Bhasa speaks to Vilasa, an old friend they meet again after years apart. Vilasa asks if Bhasa has found peace. Bhasa admits he has not. He says the mind is carried along on endless waves of tasks. It never rests for a moment. It keeps reckoning what is done, what is being done, and what must still be done. Caught in this net of reckonings, the bird of the mind faints. Years of hard effort without inner understanding leave a person exactly where they started. That same loop of running may be what you feel fraying inside you today, right in the middle of the next thing on your list.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: With a presentation tomorrow, your mind keeps imagining people laughing and thinking you do not belong in this course. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. That same restlessness can show up tonight as thoughts that loop, yet the verse names it as a real force rather than a flaw in you. You can notice the wind moving without gripping it, and let your focus rest on the words you will speak.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after hearing about a steady mind. He says the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He thinks it is as hard to hold as the wind. The verse names this struggle honestly. It proposes that practice and letting go can train the mind over time. Your mind is doing what Arjuna described. It is not a sign that you do not belong. It is simply restless, and it can be worked with.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse_text.line: I'm confused about what's right. Tell me plainly what's best; I'm ready to learn.
verse_text.translation: My nature is stricken by weakness and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me for certain what is best for me. I am your student; I have come to you, teach me.

reading: Kārpaṇya-doṣopahata-svabhāvaḥ: Arjuna says his nature is overcome, he's confused about what's right, and he asks plainly to be taught. Clarity in the Gita starts here, with someone honest enough to say 'I don't know'.
meaning: Arjuna stands on the battlefield and tells Krishna that his courage has failed him. He says he is confused about what is right. He asks Krishna to tell him plainly what is best. He offers himself as a student who has come to learn. You are caught between two costly paths and your own judgment feels too worn to trust right now.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse_text.line: I'm confused about what's right. Tell me plainly what's best; I'm ready to learn.
verse_text.translation: My nature is stricken by weakness and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me for certain what is best for me. I am your student; I have come to you, teach me.

reading: You are caught between bringing your mother to you or returning to Patna, unable to decide. Arjuna tells Krishna that his nature is stricken by weakness and his mind is confused about what is right, and he asks plainly to be taught what is best. Today, your own uncertainty about this move can be the honest starting point for seeking clarity, just as Arjuna did when he admitted he did not know.
meaning: Arjuna stands on the battlefield and tells Krishna that his nature is stricken by weakness and his mind is confused about what is right. He asks Krishna to tell him for certain what is best and to teach him, since he has come as a student. The verse proposes that clarity begins when a person admits that their own judgement has failed and humbly asks for guidance. Your own uncertainty about whether to bring your mother here or return to Patna can be the honest starting point for seeking clarity, just as Arjuna admitted he did not know.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse_text.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
verse_text.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.

reading: Seeing your batchmate promoted while you were not brings a sharp hurt, and the words feel hard to offer him. Krishna tells Arjuna to lift himself by his own self and not let himself sink, because the self alone is the friend of the self and the self alone is its enemy. Today, you can let that voice of comparison push you down, or you can treat yourself as the one who gently pulls you up toward the next step.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield while Arjuna stands in doubt and grief. Krishna tells him that a person must lift themselves by their own effort and not let themselves sink. The self alone is the true friend of the self, and the self alone is its enemy. The choice of which one to be lies with the person. Right now that comparison is telling you that you are behind, and that voice can become your own worst enemy.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You keep buying things and upgrading, yet nothing fills the hollow. Young Rama asks what a kingdom or any pleasure is to him, and who he really is. This emptiness you feel can be the doorway to asking what truly matters, rather than another upgrade.
meaning: Young Rama has just returned from his travels. He sits in his father's court. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask him why he seems so low. Rama answers that he no longer finds interest in anything around him. He asks what a kingdom means to him, and what pleasures are worth. He asks who he really is, and what all this is for. He says if the world is unreal, let it be unreal. He wants to know whose it is, and what anyone has truly gained. You are doing exactly what Rama did. You named the hollow without rushing to fill it.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: Since your company shut down, you have applied to 200 jobs and found nothing. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. In your stillness today, that same weight is allowed to be present without judgment. The bow rests in your hand, and the chariot waits exactly where you are.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra from the battlefield. Arjuna has just argued that killing his own kin would destroy families and their ways of life. He says he would rather be killed unarmed. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna sinks down on the seat of the chariot. He lets fall his bow and arrows. His mind is overwhelmed by grief. You are in a stretch where the ground feels removed, and the weight of two hundred rejections has settled into your chest.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You come home to an empty apartment, eat, sleep, and repeat, with no one to share it and no sure sense of what any of it is for. Young Rama asks what a kingdom or pleasure means to him, and who he is, and what all this is for. That same restlessness can meet you today as a real question rather than a dead end, pointing toward who you might be when the routine finally loosens its hold.
meaning: Young Rama has just returned from his travels and sits in his father's court. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask him why he seems so low. Rama answers by asking what a kingdom or any pleasure means to him. He asks who he really is and what all this is for. He suggests that if this world is unreal, let it be unreal, and asks whose it is and what anyone has gained. The text treats this honest questioning as the first healthy step toward inquiry, not as a final answer or a problem to fix. Your empty apartment and the loop of eat and sleep carry the same restlessness Rama names. That question about what any of it is for is not a failure. It is the opening move.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Censure of Craving': the poet to his own hope.
verse_text.line: I swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart. Hope, how much longer will you make me dance?
verse_text.translation: I somehow put up with the taunts of the wicked while trying to please them; I held back my tears and laughed with an empty heart; I folded my hands even before people whose minds were numbed by money. Hope, futile hope, how much more will you make me dance?

reading: You trained your own nephew, only to watch him take your biggest clients and open his own shop. Bhartrihari cries out to Hope that he swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart, asking how much longer the hope will make him dance. Today, that forced smile over your own loss may still be playing out; the verse names the hollow performance, not your worth.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines to his own hope from the Censure of Craving. He tells it that he put up with the taunts of wicked people while trying to please them. He held back his tears and laughed with an empty heart. He folded his hands before those whose minds were numbed by money. He asks how much longer hope will make him dance in this futile way. You gave your time to someone you trusted, and now you watch him take what you built. The verse names the hollow performance you may still be doing, not your worth.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: You mentioned road rage flaring at a signal until your hands shook. Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born; from attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger. The verse suggests your outburst may trace back to something you kept turning over before the drive. Notice the signal and your hands after the scream.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna what a person of steady wisdom looks like in speech, posture and walk. Krishna answers that such a person is content within and unshaken by sorrow. He then traces how a person dwells on objects and grows attached to them. That attachment hardens into wanting, and when wanting is blocked it turns into anger and ruin. Your outburst at the signal may trace back to something you kept turning over before the drive.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: You get irritated so fast these days. Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person keeps dwelling on something, attachment is born, then desire, and blocked desire turns into anger. Your irritation may be lighting up now, but the verse points to the earlier habit of turning something over in your mind until it becomes a need. Notice where your attention has been resting before the flare, and let that observation be your next step.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna has just asked what a person of steady wisdom looks like in speech, posture and walk. Krishna answers by tracing a chain. He says that when a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From that attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger. Your irritation may be lighting up now, but the verse points to the earlier habit of turning something over in your mind until it becomes a need.
